newsitem.title: USA: Reynolds Metals presses on to cut costs.
newsitem.headline: Reynolds Metals presses on to cut costs.

text.p: Reynolds Metals' financial headaches may be far from over despite unveiling ways to cut costs this year, analysts said.
On Tuesday Reynolds announced a loss of 13 cents per share in the fourth quarter of 1996 - usually their best quarter.
Alcoa, Alumax, and Alcan Aluminium all returned a profit in the same period. Kaiser Aluminum has yet to report earnings.
Losses at Reynolds would have been worse if the company had not raised $9 million or 14 cents per share from liquidating inventories.
"I thought it was a very disappointing quarter and it looks to me as if a lot of the earnings forecasts for the first quarter will have to come down," Charles Bradford of UBS Securities said.
"There is a question whether Reynolds will have any earnings per share at all in the quarter," Bradford added.
John Wilson of SBC Warburg said, "I think Reynolds has a lot of work it needs to do with its structure and it's addressing these issues."
Reynolds told analysts Tuesday it would not benefit from the run-up in aluminum prices on LME for another six months, Bradford said.
But Reynolds chairman, Jeremiah Sheehan said in a statement the company has identified 1997 savings, exclusive of any changes in aluminum prices, of $100 million pre-tax.
Further income will also come from liquidating more inventories. "The goal is to reduce inventories by $300 million over 1995 base by the end of 1999," a Reynolds spokesperson told Reuters.

Inventory assets - largely raw materials in the pipeline but also some finished product - in 1995 totaled $891 million and were cut to $787 million by the end of the fourth quarter of last year, leaving a further $196 million to reap over the next three years.
"This is part of our strategy to strengthen the balance sheet," a Reynolds spokesperson said. "This generates cash which lessens the need for short-term borrowings."
But analysts said because inventory savings were made under LIFO, it would be difficult to make gains from inventory liquidation in the first quarter.
Wilson, however, said Reynold's fourth quarter results were almost an anomaly. "The primary concern still rests with fundamental support for aluminum."
The expectation of stronger shipments this year and cost savings provided some good news, Wilson added.
But the fourth quarter losses rekindled speculation among analysts that Reynolds may be split up. Reynolds' board is due to consider in February a report on restructuring the company.
"If you were to spin off the consumer products today, the rest of the company would be deeply in the red," Bradford said. "You may have to wait until the other businesses are profitable."
Wilson said spinning off parts of Reynolds was "more of a strategic, longer term issue".
A slowdown in beer sales affected Reynolds' 1996 can shipments, but the company has now replaced one of its beer customers with a soft drinks company, seen as a sector with better growth prospects.
"We are also seeing improved demand for cans in South America," the company spokesperson said.

Some analysts have said that plastic was making inroads into aluminum's share of the beverage packaging market, but a Reynolds spokesperson said there was no evidence of this as far as the company was concerned.
